cmo-cmo-1995-01.prompt:
Let $f(x) = \dfrac{9^x}{9^x + 3}$. Evaluate the sum
$$f\left(\frac{1}{1996}\right) + f\left(\frac{2}{1996}\right) + f\left(\frac{3}{1996}\right) + \cdots + f\left(\frac{1995}{1996}\right).$$

cmo-cmo-1995-02.prompt:
Let $a$, $b$, and $c$ be positive real numbers. Prove that
$$a^a b^b c^c \ge (abc)^{\frac{a+b+c}{3}}.$$
cmo-cmo-1995-02.answer: Cube both sides: $\frac{a^{3a}b^{3b}c^{3c}}{(abc)^{a+b+c}} = \left(\frac ab\right)^{a-b}\left(\frac bc\right)^{b-c}\left(\frac ac\right)^{a-c} \ge 1$, as each factor $x^{y}$ has $x \ge 1 \iff y \ge 0$.

cmo-cmo-1995-03.prompt: Define a *boomerang* as a quadrilateral whose opposite sides do not intersect and one of whose internal angles is greater than $180$ degrees (see the figure). Let $C$ be a convex polygon having $s$ sides. Suppose that the interior region of $C$ is the union of $q$ quadrilaterals, none of whose interiors intersect one another. Also suppose that $b$ of these quadrilaterals are boomerangs. Show that $q \ge b + \frac{s-2}{2}$.
cmo-cmo-1995-03.answer: Add up all interior angles of the $q$ quadrilaterals ($2\pi q$): they include the angles at the vertices of $C$ (total $(s-2)\pi$) and, at each of the $b$ distinct reflex vertices, which lie inside $C$, a full $2\pi$.

cmo-cmo-1995-04.prompt:
Let $n$ be a fixed positive integer. Show that for all nonnegative integers $k$, the diophantine equation
$$x_1^3 + x_2^3 + \cdots + x_n^3 = y^{3k+2}$$
has infinitely many solutions in positive integers $x_i$ and $y$.
cmo-cmo-1995-04.answer: For instance $x_1 = \cdots = x_n = n^{2k+1}q^{3k+2}$, $y = n^2q^3$ ($q = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$), since $n\cdot n^{6k+3}q^{9k+6} = (n^2q^3)^{3k+2}$.

cmo-cmo-1995-05.prompt:
Suppose that $u$ is a real parameter with $0 < u < 1$. Define
$$f(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } 0 \le x \le u \\[4pt] 1 - \left(\sqrt{ux} + \sqrt{(1-u)(1-x)}\right)^2 & \text{if } u \le x \le 1 \end{cases}$$
and define the sequence $\{u_n\}$ recursively as follows:
$$u_1 = f(1), \quad\text{and}\quad u_n = f(u_{n-1}) \text{ for all } n > 1.$$
Show that there exists a positive integer $k$ for which $u_k = 0$.
cmo-cmo-1995-05.answer: $f$ maps $[0,1]$ into $[0,1]$ and $f(x) \le x - u$ for $u \le x \le 1$ (since $\sqrt{ux(1-u)(1-x)} \ge u(1-x)$), so the sequence drops by at least $u$ while it is $\ge u$; once some $u_j \le u$, the next term is $0$.
